analysis.one_liner: Rewrites the Clean Air Act to cut acid rain, urban smog, and toxic air pollution.
analysis.headline: The House passed the Clean Air Act Amendments 401-21 on May 23, 1990, then tabled the bill in favor of the Senate's companion measure, which became the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill is the House vehicle for the 1990 overhaul of the Clean Air Act. It cuts the sulfur dioxide pollution that causes acid rain by roughly 10 million tons from 1980 levels, forces states to meet firm deadlines for cleaning smog, soot, and carbon monoxide, imposes the first technology-based limits on toxic air pollutants, tightens car tailpipe standards, requires cleaner gasoline and diesel, and phases out chemicals that destroy the ozone layer. It also pays unemployment and retraining benefits to workers who lose their jobs because of the new rules.
analysis.who_benefits: People living in cities that violate smog, soot, and carbon monoxide standards, and communities downwind of coal-fired power plants that cause acid rain, get cleaner air on enforceable deadlines. Workers laid off because of compliance costs get extended unemployment and retraining assistance, and small businesses get technical help meeting permit rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of smoggy cities and acid-rain regions

how_it_helps.text: Cuts sulfur dioxide emissions by about 10 million tons below 1980 levels in two phases to stop acid rain from damaging lakes, forests, and buildings.
Classifies smoggy, sooty, and carbon monoxide areas by severity and sets firm attainment deadlines, with sanctions including loss of highway funding for states that miss them.
For the first time establishes a list of hazardous air pollutants and requires technology-based emission standards for the major industrial sources of them.

Tightens tailpipe emission standards for cars and light trucks, requires cleaner reformulated gasoline and low-sulfur diesel in polluted areas, and requires onboard systems to capture fuel vapors during refueling.
Creates an operating-permit system with public notice and comment, and makes permits, compliance plans, and monitoring reports available to the public.
Provides unemployment benefits and job training, job-search and relocation allowances to workers who lose their jobs because firms cut back to comply with the Clean Air Act.

analysis.who_pays: Electric utilities that must cut sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, refiners that must produce cleaner gasoline and diesel, automakers facing tighter tailpipe standards, and chemical and industrial plants facing toxic-emission limits, permit fees, and much larger penalties. Some of those costs pass through to households in higher electricity, gasoline, and product prices.

drawbacks.text: The acid rain program gives emission allowances to utilities at no cost, handing power plants valuable permits to keep emitting; the trading system also lets some units pollute above their own cap by buying allowances from others.

Compliance costs are real and partly reach households through higher electricity, gasoline, and diesel prices, and small businesses such as gas stations face vapor-recovery equipment and permit costs.
Timelines are long: the dirtiest ozone areas get up to twenty years to meet the standard, and visibility protections are made inapplicable east of the 100th meridian.
Emissions from oil and gas wells and pipeline compressor and pump stations cannot be aggregated to count as a major source, easing permitting requirements for the oil and gas industry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health and environmental gains are large and nationwide, while the costs fall mainly on utilities, refiners, automakers, and heavy industry, partly passed to consumers. The design leans in industry's favor in places — free allowances, long deadlines, and oil-and-gas aggregation exemptions — but it also includes worker transition assistance and strong enforcement. On balance the costs are modest relative to the public health benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 401-21, but was immediately laid on the table in favor of the Senate's companion bill, S. 1630, which went on to become the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990 — so the House bill itself never became law, though its substance did.

narrative.text: Rep. John Dingell introduced the bill on July 27, 1989 with 167 cosponsors, including 103 Republicans and 64 Democrats.
The bill spent months in subcommittee and full Energy and Commerce markup sessions before being reported by three committees in May 1990.
The House passed the bill on May 23, 1990 by a vote of 401-21, with Democrats voting 247-5 and Republicans 154-16.
The same day, the bill was laid on the table with a note to see S. 1630 for further action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people came out ahead: the substance of this bill became law later in 1990 through the Senate companion, S. 1630, so cleaner air rules took effect. The House bill was tabled only to clear the way for that Senate vehicle, not because it lacked support.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public; the law passed via S.1630

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, steered it through months of subcommittee and full-committee markup, and managed the House floor debate, including compromise substitute amendments on toxic emissions standards, CFCs, offshore platforms, and clean-fuel vehicles.

for.what_they_did: Held extensive markups across the fall of 1989 and March-April 1990, then reported the bill as amended.

sides.party_line_note: On final passage, 247 of 256 voting Democrats and 154 of 176 voting Republicans backed the bill, with only 21 members of either party opposed; cosponsorship was bipartisan too, with 103 Republicans and 64 Democrats signing on.

industries.note: Title V cuts their sulfur dioxide emissions by about 10 million tons from 1980 levels, but it issues emission allowances to them at no cost and creates a valuable tradable permit market, letting them recover costs through regulated rates. The bill regulates utilities heavily while locking in their role as the channel for acid-rain control.

Tighter tailpipe standards from model year 1994, onboard refueling vapor recovery, longer emission-control warranties, and clean-fuel fleet mandates raise manufacturing costs, which are passed into car prices. The costs are the flip side of the cleaner air the public gets.

Reformulated gasoline rules, vapor-pressure limits, and a 0.05 percent sulfur cap on highway diesel force costly changes at refineries. The ethanol blend gets a one-pound vapor-pressure tolerance, a carve-out benefiting corn-state producers.

New technology-based standards for listed hazardous air pollutants, risk-management plans for accidental releases, permit fees of at least $25 per ton, and penalties up to $1,000,000 per day for knowing hazardous releases raise compliance costs. The exemptions for oil and gas well aggregation soften the burden for that segment.

Clean-fuel vehicle programs in the worst smog areas, clean-fuel mandates for urban buses, oxygenated-fuel requirements in carbon monoxide areas, and the ethanol vapor-pressure waiver create guaranteed markets. The public benefits from cleaner fuel, but the mandates also steer demand to these producers.

Acid rain controls push power plants toward lower-sulfur coal, hurting high-sulfur coal regions, but the bill cushions them: a Governor's certification can preclude use of out-of-state coal, and incentive allowances for units in states with their own sulfur laws are conditioned on no net decrease in high-sulfur mining jobs.
